hero.legend: A sacred tree, five statues, the birth of a city. In 1372 the wealthy widow Lady Penh (Daun Penh) found a drifting Koki tree on the Tonlé Sap riverbank; within it lay four bronze Buddhas and one stone Vishnu. She led her neighbors to mound the earth into a hill and enshrine the relics — and Phnom Penh ('the hill of Penh') was founded, with Wat Phnom as the spiritual heart of the millennium-old capital.

season.title: When to visit: seasonal strategy table
season.subtitle: Weather, water and wildlife combined across Cambodia's three seasons.
season.intro: Wat Phnom sits on a low hill in central Phnom Penh, where the year divides into a cool dry season, a hot dry season and a monsoon season. The table below brings three dimensions together — climate, water conditions and wildlife activity — so you can match your visit to the conditions you actually care about.

rows.name: Cool dry season
rows.weather: The most comfortable window of the year: daytime highs around 30–32 °C, nights near 21–23 °C, low humidity and the least rainfall. Early mornings can bring light mist over the hill.
rows.water: Water levels sit at their annual low, so the pond and riverside channels are calmer and clearer and the panorama from the hilltop is at its most open.
rows.wildlife: Egrets, mynas and the temple squirrels are active in the canopy, and the bodhi and banyan trees stay green — the most reliable window for birdwatching and photography.
rows.strategy: First choice for a first visit. Both the half-day and full-day routes work well; go early morning or late afternoon, and expect the busiest crowds between 09:00 and 11:00.

rows.name: Hot dry season
rows.weather: The hottest stretch of the year: afternoon highs of 35–38 °C, strong UV, and occasional convective showers or thunderstorms late in the day.
rows.water: Levels are low, the surface drops and the chance of algae growth and turbidity rises. Treat water features as scenery only and avoid contact.
rows.wildlife: Activity shifts to dawn and dusk, with very little movement at midday. Flowering trees attract more insects and bees during this period.
rows.strategy: Ascend only between 07:00–09:30 or after 16:30. Carry sunscreen and water, keep hilltop time short, and stay clear of trees and lamp posts when a storm rolls in.

rows.name: Monsoon season
rows.weather: The southwest monsoon brings heavy rain, peaking between July and September, usually as intense afternoon downpours. Paths turn slippery and humidity often stays above 85%.
rows.water: The Mekong and Tonlé Sap rise markedly and water features refill, turbidity increases, and short-term surface ponding is possible during the heaviest rain.
rows.wildlife: After rain, frogs and insects are active in the temple grounds and birds gather in the understorey. Vegetation is at its greenest — the best stretch for rich, saturated imagery.
rows.strategy: Bring rain gear and non-slip footwear and plan around the afternoon storms. Stone steps are most slippery 30–60 minutes after rain, so hold the handrail; mist and wet stone make this a strong period for photography.

season.note: This combined assessment covers three dimensions — climate, hydrology and ecology. Climate context follows the 30-year climate normals (1991–2020) published by NOAA and the Ministry of Water Resources and Meteorology of Cambodia (MOWRAM); water and ecological observations reference public material from the Ministry of Environment of Cambodia. Conditions vary from year to year — treat this as planning guidance, not a forecast.

itineraries.title: Recommended routes: half day & full day
itineraries.subtitle: Two ready-made routes matched to the time you have.

half.title: Half-day route (3 hours)
half.summary: A compact route for travellers with limited time: straight up to the temple, around the hilltop, then back down past the landmarks that gave the city its name.

steps.title: Arrive at the foot of the hill
steps.text: Enter from the main stairway on Wat Phnom Road. If you would like to make an offering, incense and flower garlands are sold at the entrance.

steps.title: Climb the main stairway
steps.text: The wide eastern stairway is the classic approach — the naga balustrade and the avenue seen from above are the signature view.

steps.title: Hilltop temple and stupa
steps.text: Walk clockwise around the central sanctuary, then visit the small shrine of Lady Penh, the figure behind the city's name.

steps.title: Pond and memorial terrace
steps.text: Descend slowly, then circle the pond at the base and the memorial on the eastern side for a calmer view of the hill.

steps.title: Coffee or breakfast nearby
steps.text: Continue on foot towards the riverside or the central market district, where many cafés and local eateries open early.

half.tip: Best for a first visit, a layover or a travel day with a fixed departure — you can be back in the city centre within three hours.

full.title: Full-day route (7 hours)
full.summary: A route that puts the temple back into the context of the old city: hill, old market, royal palace, national museum, and a riverside finish.

steps.title: Sunrise and the hilltop
steps.text: Start with the coolest hour: temple, stupa and the hilltop panorama before the coach groups arrive.

steps.title: Breakfast stop
steps.text: Local breakfast shops and cafés sit within a short walk of the hill — noodle soups, coffee and fresh fruit.

steps.title: Old market and heritage streets
steps.text: Explore the surrounding streets: colonial-era shophouses, art-deco market buildings and the city's historic trading quarter.

steps.title: Royal Palace & Silver Pagoda
steps.text: A 15–20 minute walk or a short ride south reaches the palace complex, the most important royal site in the country.

steps.title: Lunch and rest
steps.text: Take a long, air-conditioned lunch break during the hottest part of the day.

steps.title: National Museum
steps.text: Khmer art and sculpture, a few minutes from the palace and a useful complement to the iconography of the temple.

steps.title: Riverside and sunset
steps.text: Finish along the Tonlé Sap and Mekong promenade as the light softens over the water.

full.tip: Best if you want to see the temple in the context of the historic city centre — visit the hill first, then let the day flow south and east towards the river.

itineraries.note: Walking times assume a relaxed pace with photo stops. Tuk-tuks and ride-hailing apps are widely available if you prefer to shorten any leg.

audience.title: Three routes tailored to how you travel
audience.subtitle: Pick the plan that matches your group and your pace.

items.title: Families with children
items.summary: A short, low-pressure visit built around the stairway, the open hilltop and the pond, with plenty of shade and seating.
points: Climb the main stairway in short stages — there is room to stop on every landing.
Hold children's hands on the stone steps, which are worn smooth in places and slippery after rain.
Keep to the hilltop and the pond terrace; skipping the western side keeps walking distances short.
Carry water and a hat, and use the shaded benches at the base for breaks.
items.tip: Best before 09:30 or after 16:30 — cooler, quieter and easier on young children.

items.title: Photographers & nature lovers
items.summary: A light-driven plan that follows the best angles on the hill and through the surrounding greenery.
points: Early morning gives soft side light on the eastern stairway and mist among the trees.
Late afternoon brings warm light onto the temple façade and the city skyline beyond the hill.
The tree canopy around the base is the most productive area for birds and squirrels.
Compose the naga balustrade, the stupa spire and the avenue below as your three signature frames.
items.tip: Rainy-season afternoons add saturated greens and reflective stone — worth the trip if you can dodge the heaviest downpours.

items.title: Low-mobility & step-free visiting
items.summary: A plan for visitors who prefer to avoid long stairways, using the gentler approach and the manageable parts of the site.
points: A paved access road winds up the eastern side of the hill with a much gentler gradient than the stairs.
The plateau at the top is level and can be explored without climbing further steps.
Seating and shade are available at the base of the hill and around the plateau.
If you use a wheelchair or have limited stamina, ask staff or your driver to approach from the upper road.
items.tip: Arriving by vehicle close to the plateau removes almost all of the climb; mornings are the quietest and coolest window.

responsibility.title: Site science and visitor responsibilities
responsibility.subtitle: What makes this hill a landmark — and how to leave it as you found it.

knowItems.t: A hill built on a legend
knowItems.d: The city takes its name from Lady Penh (Daun Penh), who is said to have found four bronze Buddha statues on a floating tree on the river and raised a hill to enshrine them — giving Phnom Penh its name, 'the hill of Lady Penh'.
The sanctuary is an active place of worship rather than a museum. Monks reside here and daily prayers continue, so visitors share the space with worshippers.
The main stupa was enlarged several times between the 15th and 19th centuries and rebuilt in the 1920s, so what you see today combines Khmer religious architecture with later repair work.

knowItems.t: A low hill in a low-lying city
knowItems.d: At roughly 27 metres, the hill is the only significant elevation in the city centre — which is why it works as a viewpoint, an orientation landmark and the focal point of the area's greenery.

dutyItems.d: Cover shoulders and knees, remove hats inside the sanctuary, speak quietly, and avoid pointing your feet towards Buddha images.

dutyItems.t: Do not feed or disturb wildlife
dutyItems.d: Feeding birds, squirrels or monkeys changes their behaviour and diet and can create dependency; observe and photograph from a distance instead.
Packaging and plastic bottles should leave the hill with you — waste infrastructure on site is still limited.
Do not enter or handle the pond or the river edge; water quality is affected by seasonal runoff and urban drainage.

dutyItems.t: Keep drones, flash and tripods discreet
dutyItems.d: Drones are not appropriate over a working religious site; ask before using a tripod or flash around worshippers.
Donations, offerings or purchases from the small stalls help maintain the temple — and are always optional.

pocketGuide.qaHint: The questions most visitors search for before arriving.

qa.q: How much is the entrance fee to Wat Phnom?
qa.a: Entering the temple grounds is free of charge; donations for incense, flowers or oil lamps are welcome but voluntary. A small upkeep fee (around 500–1,000 riel) may be asked at some public toilets, so keep a little cash.
The site is generally open daily from about 07:00 to 19:00. Arrive before 09:00 or after 16:00 for softer light and fewer crowds; during Khmer New Year and Pchum Ben it is far busier.

qa.q: How high is the hill and how many steps are there?
qa.a: The hill rises roughly 27 m above the surrounding streets — the main stairway on the east side is the traditional way up. A paved service road on the east offers a much gentler climb if you prefer fewer steps.

qa.q: How do I get there from the Royal Palace or the riverside?
qa.a: It is about 1.5–2 km north of the Royal Palace and the riverside promenade: roughly 20–25 minutes on foot, or 5–10 minutes by tuk-tuk. The temple sits at the Norodom Boulevard and Street 96 roundabout.

qa.q: Where does the name Daun Penh come from?
qa.a: According to local tradition, in 1372 a wealthy widow named Penh found four Buddha statues inside a koki tree floating on the Mekong. A hill was raised to enshrine them, giving the temple — and the district — the name Daun Penh, 'Hill of Lady Penh'.

qa.q: What should I wear, and can I take photos?
qa.a: Cover shoulders and knees and remove shoes and hats before entering the vihear. Photography of the buildings and statues is fine, but ask before photographing people praying, and never point your feet towards a Buddha image.

history.title: History & Significance of Wat Phnom Daun Penh
history.subtitle: From a 14th-century legend to the spiritual heart of Phnom Penh.

sections.heading: The legend of Lady Penh
sections.body: A wealthy widow, Lady Penh (Daun Penh, 'Grandmother Penh'), found four bronze Buddha statues — and one stone Vishnu — hidden inside a drifting Koki tree on the riverbank. She summoned her neighbors to mound earth into a hill (phnom) and enshrine the relics in a wooden shrine. The act gave the city its name: Phnom Penh, 'the hill of Penh'.

sections.heading: Capital moves to Phnom Penh
sections.body: King Ponhea Yat relocated the Khmer capital from Angkor to Phnom Penh. He rebuilt Wat Phnom and raised a great white stupa (chedi) on the summit to house his ashes. The humble hill shrine was elevated into a royal spiritual center.

sections.heading: A growing sacred hill
sections.body: Across centuries the shrine was repeatedly rebuilt and enlarged. The artificial hill became the focus of local faith, and the surrounding settlement gradually grew into today's capital.

sections.heading: French Protectorate care
sections.body: Under the French Protectorate, successive kings restored and expanded the temple. The stupa and vihear (prayer hall) took on the later Khmer restoration style still seen today.

sections.heading: Hébrard's restoration
sections.body: The renowned architect Ernest Hébrard led a major restoration during the colonial period, shaping the classic silhouette of Wat Phnom that visitors recognize today.

sections.heading: Symbol of the capital
sections.body: Today Wat Phnom stands as a national cultural emblem and the namesake hill of Phnom Penh, welcoming devotees and travelers from around the world.

history.legendTitle: The founding legend of Lady Penh
history.legendText: The tale of Lady Penh and the drifting Koki tree is Phnom Penh's best-loved origin story. Inside the tree she found four bronze Buddhas and a stone Vishnu — a quiet sign of how Cambodian Buddhism blended with earlier Hindu devotion. The mound she raised became the hill, and her shrine became the temple that still gives the capital its name.

architecture.title: Khmer Buddhist architecture
architecture.subtitle: A layered hilltop sanctuary: stupa, shrines, murals and sacred trees.

features.title: Central stupa
features.text: The tall white stupa enshrines sacred relics and marks the spiritual center of the hill.

features.title: Buddha images
features.text: Revered Buddha statues — including those tied to the founding legend — are enshrined within the vihear.

features.title: Vihear murals
features.text: Painted in the early 20th century, the hall murals depict the Buddha's Jataka tales woven with scenes from the Khmer epic Reamker (Ramayana). Look up: the ceiling shows a cosmic mandala and the pillars are sheathed in gold.

features.title: Khmer ornament
features.text: Naga balustrades, lotus motifs and carved lintels showcase classic Khmer craftsmanship.

features.title: Seven-headed Naga stair
features.text: The dramatic stairway guarded by a seven-headed naga (serpent) symbolises the rainbow bridge linking the human world to the cosmos (Mount Meru) — a stairway to the heavens.

features.title: Sacred tree & shrines
features.text: Shaded trees and Lady Penh's small votive shrine dot the hilltop, lending a calm, contemplative atmosphere.

features.title: Hilltop layout
features.text: The man-made hill lifts the temple above the streets, offering a quiet overlook of the city.

features.title: Preah Chau Shrine
features.text: On the hill's north side stands the Chinese sanctuary (Preah Chau), where Khmer, Chinese and Vietnamese folk faiths meet. Merchants and students come to pray for wealth, success in studies, or draw a fortune stick (kien).

faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.subtitle: Quick answers to plan your Wat Phnom visit.

items.q: Where is Wat Phnom Daun Penh located?
items.a: Wat Phnom Daun Penh is located in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, on the hill at the end of Wat Phnom Road in the Daun Penh district.

items.q: Is Wat Phnom free to visit?
items.a: Wat Phnom Daun Penh is a public temple space and is free to enter year-round; donations to support the temple are welcome.

items.q: What are the opening hours of Wat Phnom?
items.a: The hilltop temple is generally open daily from 07:00 to 19:00. Please confirm on-site information before travelling.
Yes — it is one of Phnom Penh's most important cultural landmarks and the namesake hill of the city.

items.q: How long should I spend at Wat Phnom?
items.a: Most visitors spend 30 minutes to 1 hour on the hilltop, temple and views.
Dress modestly covering shoulders and knees when visiting the temple.

items.q: How do I get to Wat Phnom?
items.a: Wat Phnom sits in central Phnom Penh near the Norodom Boulevard and Street 96 roundabout, roughly 15–20 minutes on foot from the riverside.

items.q: When is the best time to visit?
items.a: Early morning is cool and less crowded; evening light is warm with a strong city atmosphere.

items.q: How high is Wat Phnom hill, and how many steps are there?
items.a: The hill rises about 27 m above the surrounding streets. The main stairway on the east side is the traditional route up; a paved service road offers a much gentler climb if you prefer fewer steps.

items.q: What is there to see near Wat Phnom?
items.a: The Royal Palace and Silver Pagoda and the riverside promenade are about 1.5–2 km south, and the Central Market (Phsar Thmei) is around 1.2 km west — all reachable on foot or by a short tuk-tuk ride.

items.q: Can I take photos at Wat Phnom?
items.a: Photographing the buildings and Buddha images is generally fine, but ask before photographing people praying, and avoid pointing your feet towards Buddha images.

amenities.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Facilities
amenities.subtitle: A neutral, type-only reference for planning your visit — facilities are described by category, never by business name.

cards.title: Restrooms
cards.text: Public toilets at the southeast base of the hill and near the main stairway entrance. A small upkeep fee (≈500–1,000 riel) may apply — bring small change and tissues.

cards.title: Parking & Drop-off
cards.text: Tuk-tuk / ride-hail drop-off around the roundabout (Norodom Blvd × St 96). Motorbikes park in marked bays with an attendant; cars/buses use nearby commercial or underground parking, then walk 3–5 min.

cards.title: Dining & Refreshments
cards.text: Street vendors by the park path sell fresh coconut water, chilled bottled water and Khmer snacks. Cafés and air-conditioned restaurants line Norodom Blvd within 3–8 min walk.

cards.title: Accommodation Areas
cards.text: Grouped only by district for neutrality: Riverside (~800m–1.5km), Norodom Blvd / Central (~500m–2km), and Central Market area (~1–1.5km). No specific hotels named.

cards.title: Convenience & Supplies
cards.text: 24-hour convenience stores within 500m for sunscreen, tissues, mosquito repellent and water. Phsar Thmei (Central Market) is ~1.2km away for fruit and daily goods.

cards.title: Fuel & EV Charging
cards.text: Standard fuel stations line Monivong/Norodom Blvds. EV charging is concentrated in shopping-mall basements and some modern stations; nearest hub is a commercial plaza ~5–10 min by car.

cards.title: Drinking Water
cards.text: Sealed bottled water is sold by vendors and shops along the approach path, and a few cafés will refill your bottle if you ask. Municipal tap water is not recommended for drinking — buy sealed or filtered water.

cards.title: Step-free Access
cards.text: The stairways are the classic approach, but a paved service lane on the eastern side has a much gentler gradient. For the shortest walk, ask staff or your driver to come in from the upper road side; the hilltop plateau itself is level.

cards.title: Pharmacy & Medical
cards.text: Pharmacies carrying everyday medicine and basic first-aid supplies sit along the surrounding boulevards, roughly 5–10 minutes away on foot. Private clinics and the city's larger hospitals are a 10–20 minute drive.

cards.title: Cash, Cards & ATMs
cards.text: ATMs and bank branches are within a few minutes' walk on the surrounding boulevards. Cards are widely accepted in shops and cafés, but small riel notes remain handy for offerings, drinks and restroom upkeep fees.

cards.title: Connectivity & Charging
cards.text: Free Wi-Fi is common in nearby cafés and shopping centres, and a local SIM or eSIM gives fast, inexpensive mobile data. Public charging points on the hill are rare, so pack a power bank.

cards.title: Luggage & Baby Facilities
cards.text: There is no official cloakroom on the hill; nearby cafés, hotels and shopping centres are the usual places to leave bags. Baby-changing facilities exist in modern shopping centres rather than at the temple.

cards.title: Information & Assistance
cards.text: There is no separate visitor centre — the entrance and the temple office are the usual points of contact for directions, offerings and basic guidance.

cards.title: Rain & Sun Gear
cards.text: Compact umbrellas, ponchos and sun hats are sold by vendors close to the entrance and are genuinely useful during the monsoon months. Sunscreen is available from convenience stores nearby.

cards.title: Safety & Emergencies
cards.text: The area is busy and generally safe during opening hours. Keep bags in front of you in crowds, take worn stone steps slowly, and use the national emergency lines if needed — police 117, ambulance 119.

tips.label: Shorter walk
tips.value: Gentler paved lane on the east side

tips.label: Payment
tips.value: Cards accepted; keep small riel notes
